mcqs.question: What happens, at the hardware level, when a user-mode program tries to execute a privileged instruction?
options: The CPU raises a general protection fault, handing control to the kernel to decide what to do
The instruction silently executes but has no effect
The CPU automatically switches the process into kernel mode to complete it
The instruction is queued and retried once the process gains permission
mcqs.explanation: Hardware enforces the privilege check directly: an illegal instruction in user mode triggers a fault that traps into the kernel, which typically kills the offending process. It doesn't execute silently, auto-promote the process, or get queued for later.

mcqs.question: x86 hardware defines four protection rings (0-3). Which two do general-purpose OSes like Linux and Windows actually use?
options: Ring 1 and Ring 2, reserving 0 and 3 for hypervisors only
All four rings are used equally for different driver classes
Ring 0 for the kernel and Ring 3 for everything else
Ring 0 and Ring 1, treating them as equally privileged
mcqs.explanation: Mainstream OSes use only the two extremes — Ring 0 (kernel) and Ring 3 (user applications) — skipping the middle rings for simplicity, even though the hardware defines four. Rings 1 and 2 exist in the spec but see little real-world use in general-purpose OSes.

mcqs.question: Why can't a user process just jump directly to arbitrary kernel code to request a service?
options: Kernel code is stored on disk and must be loaded first
The trap instruction forces entry only at a fixed, kernel-chosen handler address, not one the caller supplies
User processes are physically incapable of executing any jump instruction
The kernel only accepts requests during a specific time window each second
mcqs.explanation: The trap mechanism's entire security value is that the entry point into kernel mode is fixed by the kernel, never chosen by the calling code — that's what prevents a process from forging its way into arbitrary privileged code. Kernel code is resident in memory, jumps work fine in user mode, and there's no time-window restriction.

mcqs.question: A web server process crashes but every other process on the machine keeps running normally. What does this tell you about where the fault occurred?
options: The fault occurred in kernel mode, since only kernel faults are recoverable
This behavior is impossible — any crash always requires a full reboot
The scheduler must have been in real-time mode at the time
The fault occurred in user mode, since kernel isolation contained it to one process
mcqs.explanation: A contained crash that doesn't affect other processes is the signature of a user-mode fault — the kernel simply reclaims that process's resources. A kernel-mode fault (panic) affects the whole machine, the opposite of what's described here, and reboots aren't universal for user crashes.

mcqs.question: A service does a `write()` syscall once per row while inserting a million rows, and profiling shows most time in `%sys`. What's the likely fix?
options: Switch the service to a faster programming language
Buffer writes and issue far fewer, larger syscalls instead of one per row
Increase the process's scheduling priority
Add more CPU cores to the machine
mcqs.explanation: Each syscall pays real mode-switch overhead (register save/restore, pipeline effects); doing a million tiny syscalls instead of a few large buffered ones is a classic hot-path mistake. Language choice, priority, and core count don't address the per-call mode-switch tax being paid a million times.

mcqs.question: How does a debugger like gdb inspect and control another process's memory and registers without breaking user/kernel isolation?
options: It runs the target process in kernel mode temporarily
It directly maps the target process's memory into its own address space with no kernel involvement
It disables the CPU's mode bit for the duration of the debug session
It uses the ptrace syscall, a kernel-mediated interface built specifically for controlled inspection
mcqs.explanation: ptrace is a kernel-provided, permissioned interface — the kernel still mediates every access, preserving isolation. There's no temporary kernel-mode promotion of the target, no direct unmediated memory mapping, and the CPU's mode bit isn't something software can just switch off.
